answer_text:
Yes, absolutely! Teacher shortages are a widespread and growing problem in the United States. Here is a breakdown of the most affected academic fields:

---

## 📚 Academic Fields with the Most Severe Teacher Shortages

### The Overall Picture
An estimated 410,000+ teaching positions — representing 1 in 8 of all teaching positions nationally — are either unfilled or filled by teachers not fully certified for their assignments. In the 2024–25 school year, every state and the District of Columbia reported shortages in more than one teaching area.

---

### 1. 🧠 Special Education
The shortage of Special Education educators is the greatest, with a documented shortage in 44 of 50 states. Special education remains one of the most in-demand teaching subjects due to the growing need for qualified educators. Over the past 45 years, the number of students in special education programs has doubled, while retention of special education teachers has become a persistent issue, with many leaving due to burnout or insufficient resources.

---

### 2. ➕ Mathematics
There is a shortage of math educators in 38 out of 50 states. The National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP) reports that mathematics and science proficiency continue to drop among fourth and eighth graders, making the need for qualified math teachers even more urgent.

---

### 3. 🔬 Science (STEM)
The shortage is particularly acute in STEM fields and foreign languages. According to the U.S. Department of Education, over half of all states (37) report a shortage of qualified STEM teachers, with high-need, low-income schools affected the most.

---

### 4. 🌐 ESL / TESOL (English as a Second Language)
TESOL (Teaching English to Speakers of Other Languages) is a high-need area for teachers as the population of English Language Learners (ELLs) and Multilingual Learners (MLs) in U.S. schools grows. Projections indicate that by 2030, 40% of students in K-12 classrooms will be ELLs/MLs.

---

### 5. 📖 Language Arts / English
The largest concentrations of shortage positions were in special education, elementary education, language arts, and career and technical education, measured by vacancies, temporary certifications, and out-of-field assignments.

---

### 6. 🔧 Career and Technical Education (CTE)
The numbers of shortage positions were deepest in special education, elementary education, language arts, and career and technical education. These teaching areas account for the highest numbers of teacher shortages nationwide.

---

### 7. 🏫 Elementary Education (General)
Shortages range from general elementary teachers to those in career and technical education in secondary schools.

---

## Why Are There So Many Shortages?

Teacher attrition accounts for approximately 90% of annual demand for new teachers. Importantly, most educators who leave are not retiring — instead, they cite factors such as inadequate pay, limited professional support, challenging working conditions, and dissatisfaction with their roles.

States most commonly reported shortage areas in special education (45 states), science (41 states), and math (40 states). Collectively, 48 states reported shortages in at least one of these three teaching areas — areas that have had shortages since at least 1990, when the Department of Education began collecting these data.

These shortages are a long-standing and worsening crisis, making teaching in any of these fields a career with strong job security and, in many cases, access to loan forgiveness and financial incentives.
